case_prompt:
An 8‑month‑old previously healthy boy was admitted to an outside hospital with a high fever and cough of several weeks’ duration. Initial work‑up showed elevated C‑reactive protein and a nonspecific chest‑x‑ray infiltrate; he received beta‑lactam and glycopeptide antibiotics. Hemoglobin (5.6‑7.8 mmol/L) and platelets (90‑125 × 10⁹/L) were reduced; other laboratory values were unremarkable. Blood, cerebrospinal fluid, urine cultures and PCRs for respiratory viruses and atypical pneumonia pathogens were negative. Because fever persisted, he was transferred to three additional hospitals, ultimately to a tertiary centre where immunodeficiency was evaluated. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation due to declining condition. His respiratory status worsened, and after four weeks from first presentation he was transferred to our institution for veno‑venous ECMO support.

On arrival he was deeply sedated (Glasgow coma score 3/15) with a temperature of 40.3 °C, heart rate 142 bpm, blood pressure 82/44 mmHg (on epinephrine 2 µg/kg/min), weight 7.9 kg (15th percentile), length 70 cm (30th percentile), and SpO₂ 70 %. Ventilator settings were peak inspiratory pressure 60 cm H₂O, PEEP 12 cm H₂O, FiO₂ 1.0, frequency 40 /min, Horovitz quotient 30. The spleen (5 cm) and liver (6 cm) were palpable.

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (hemoglobin 4.3 mmol/L, leukocytes 2.6 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 0.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 32 × 10⁹/L), CRP 194 mg/L, ferritin 1 020 µg/L, triglycerides 3.58 mmol/L, and soluble IL‑2 receptor 30 247 U/mL. Arterial blood gases showed pH 6.9, pCO₂ 93 mmHg, pO₂ 30 mmHg, base excess –11.1 mmol/L. Chest x‑ray demonstrated a “white lung”; abdominal ultrasound showed hepato‑ and splenomegaly. Bone‑marrow biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytosis. Immunophenotyping showed CD3⁺ 1 358 × 10⁹/L, CD4⁺ 1 119 × 10⁹/L, CD8⁺ 2 017 × 10⁹/L, CD19⁺ 487 × 10⁹/L, CD56⁺ 2 × 10⁹/L; NK‑cell degranulation was normal (14.7 %). Hair microscopy was normal.

Cultures of blood, urine, tracheal secretions and stool were negative. Serologies and PCRs for a broad panel of viruses (EBV, HIV, CMV, hanta, adenovirus, influenza A/B, RSV, HSV, coronavirus, metapneumovirus, parvovirus B19, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, enterovirus) were all negative. Tests for leishmania, legionella, aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Haemophilus influenzae b and pneumococcus (PCR/IgG/IgM) were negative. Tumor markers (AFP, NSE, β‑hCG, homovanillic acid, vanillylmandelic acid) were uninformative.

A positive interferon‑gamma release assay (IGRA) was obtained on day 12, representing the first indication of possible Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hemophagocytosis met criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, prompting a search for an underlying trigger. | "Bone marrow biopsy showed a distinct hemophagocytosis…"
2. Hereditary HLH was excluded by normal NK‑cell degranulation and normal perforin, CD27, SAP, XIAP expression. | "Normal fresh degranulation of natural killer cells (14.7%; normal: >10%)… normal expressions of perforin, CD27, SAP, and XIAP…"
3. Common bacterial sepsis was unlikely because repeated blood, urine, and tracheal cultures were negative despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Results of infectious work‑up… remained negative."
4. Viral etiologies were ruled out by comprehensive negative serologies and PCRs for EBV, HIV, CMV, and other respiratory viruses. | "All serological and PCR tests for viruses… were negative."
5. Fungal infections such as aspergillosis and Pneumocystis pneumonia were excluded by negative PCR/antigen tests. | "All testing for leishmania, legionella, aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii… were negative."
6. Parasitic infections (leishmania) were excluded by negative serology and PCR. | "All testing for leishmania… were negative."
7. Malignancy was considered but tumor markers (AFP, NSE, β‑hCG, HVA, VMA) were unrevealing, and imaging could not be performed. | "All tumors markers… were unrevealing."
8. Tuberculosis became a leading candidate after a positive IGRA, despite initial negative acid‑fast stain and PCR on early BAL samples. | "A positive result from the interferon‑gamma release assay (IGRA) was the first indication for possible TBC infection on d 12."
9. The eventual confirmation of M. tuberculosis by culture and PCR (performed later) validated TB as the trigger of secondary HLH. | (Later in the course, PCR for TBC became positive and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid culture returned positive results on d 40.)

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case provides sufficient clinical, laboratory, and imaging data to establish Pneumocystis pneumonia, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (pneumocystis).  
2. Breakpoint: End the case prompt after the CT‑pulmonary angiogram description that notes diffuse ground‑glass changes suggestive of PCP, but before the bronchoalveolar lavage PCR result that definitively identifies Pneumocystis jirovecii. This includes all preceding symptoms, exam findings, labs (notably elevated beta‑D‑glucan), and imaging that allow the learner to infer PCP without the explicit PCR confirmation.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded pulmonary embolism (CTPA negative), bacterial/viral pneumonias (viral PCR panel negative), mycobacterial infection (negative test), and invasive fungal disease (galactomannan negative, cytology unremarkable). The combination of immunosuppression, elevated β‑D‑glucan, and a peripheral ground‑glass pattern on CT directed them toward PCP, later confirmed by PCR.
case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old Caucasian man, a live‑donor kidney transplant recipient, presented with several weeks of dyspnoea and tachycardia on minimal exertion. He denied other systemic symptoms. Examination revealed a regular pulse of 95 bpm at rest, rising to 120 bpm on walking, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, SpO₂ 98% on room air, and mild bilateral pitting edema to the ankles. He also had multiple slowly progressive skin patches over the past six months.

His immunosuppressive regimen included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and low‑dose prednisolone. Laboratory studies showed a normal neutrophil count, lymphopenia (0.74 ×10⁹/L), normocytic anemia (Hb 11.0 g/dL), slight elevations in C‑reactive protein (14.4 mg/L) and ESR (14 mm 1st hr), and a β‑D‑glucan level >523 pg/mL (positive >80 pg/mL). Renal function was stable (creatinine 120 µmol/L, eGFR 64 mL/min/1.73 m²). Viral PCR panels for HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, BK virus, SARS‑CoV‑2, and other respiratory pathogens were negative; serologies for toxoplasma and leishmania were also negative. Urinalysis and ECG were unremarkable; echocardiogram showed no cardiac pathology and chest X‑ray was normal.

During the same period, he developed sudden painless bilateral visual blurring. Visual acuity was 6/36 (right) and 6/60 (left). Fundoscopy revealed mild nasal disc margin blurring, small patches of retinal pallor, cotton‑wool spots, and intraretinal hemorrhages across the posterior pole and mid‑periphery in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography showed bilateral hyper‑reflective patches at the inner nuclear layer, and fluorescein angiography demonstrated an enlarged foveal avascular zone with early patchy hyperfluorescence. A diagnosis of Purtscher‑like retinopathy (PLR) was made.

A CT‑pulmonary angiogram was performed to evaluate dyspnoea. It excluded pulmonary embolism but demonstrated faint diffuse ground‑glass opacities, more prominent in the perihilar regions, described as “suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia.”
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pulmonary embolism considered due to tachycardia and dyspnoea but ruled out by CTPA “excluded pulmonary embolism as the cause for dyspnoea and sinus tachycardia.”  
2. Bacterial pneumonia considered; lack of fever, normal chest X‑ray, and absence of lobar infiltrates made it less likely; authors did not report a positive sputum culture.  
3. Viral pneumonias (including COVID‑19, CMV, EBV) were evaluated; viral PCR panel “all turned out negative.”  
4. Mycobacterial infection investigated; “Tests for mycobacteria … were negative,” reducing its likelihood.  
5. Invasive fungal infection (e.g., aspergillosis) assessed via galactomannan; “galactomannan antigen were negative,” arguing against it.  
6. Drug‑induced lung disease (e.g., from immunosuppressants) considered but no temporal drug changes and imaging pattern was atypical.  
7. Pneumocystis pneumonia became the leading diagnosis because of immunosuppression, markedly elevated β‑D‑glucan “>523 pg/mL (positive > 80 pg/mL),” and the CT finding of “faint diffuse ground glass changes … suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia.”  
8. The definitive confirmation later came from PCR detection of Pneumocystis jirovecii, but the pre‑PCR data already strongly supported PCP as the most probable etiology.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder presenting as generalized weakness, ultimately diagnosed as Lambert‑Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). LEMS is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so it is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all data up to and including the detailed electrophysiological study (repetitive nerve stimulation showing a significant incremental response) but stop before the authors interpret these findings as “suggesting a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder (likely LEMS)” and before initiating IVIG. This provides sufficient clues (weakness pattern, normal NCS/EMG with poor recruitment, incremental response) for learners to deduce LEMS without explicit naming.  
3. A 55‑year‑old woman from Mugu, a visceral leishmaniasis‑endemic district in western Nepal, presented to the outpatient department with a 2‑year history of multiple, progressively enlarging, painless nodular lesions confined to her tongue. She reported mild dysphagia but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Examination revealed several well‑circumscribed, erythematous, round‑to‑oval nodules, 1–2 cm in diameter, on the dorsal and lateral tongue surfaces; the nodules were smooth, non‑ulcerated, and not bleeding. No hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or cutaneous lesions elsewhere were detected. Differential diagnoses considered initially included infectious diseases such as Hansen’s disease and tuberculosis, as well as mucosal neuromas, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, and mycosis fungoides.

An incisional biopsy of a tongue lesion showed hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium overlying a dense dermal infiltrate with fibrotic stroma and striated muscle fibers. The submucosa contained a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes with multiple well‑formed epithelioid granulomas, involving the striated muscle. No Leishman‑Donovan bodies were seen on hematoxylin‑eosin or Giemsa stains. A slit‑skin smear for Giemsa staining could not be obtained because of the tongue’s rich vascularity, so tissue biopsy was prioritized.

Despite the absence of a prior visceral leishmaniasis diagnosis, leishmaniasis remained a consideration based on endemicity and the granulomatous histology. rK‑39 serology was positive, although its sensitivity in mucosal PKDL is limited. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting L. donovani DNA was performed. Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli and Congo red. HIV serology was negative. No histologic or clinical features suggested mycosis fungoides.

1. Hansen’s disease considered because of chronic nodular oral lesions in an endemic region; excluded by lack of characteristic nerve enlargement, negative slit‑smear for acid‑fast bacilli, and granulomas without acid‑fast organisms. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included infectious diseases such as Hansen's disease and tuberculosis... Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli..."
2. Tuberculosis considered given granulomatous inflammation; excluded by negative acid‑fast stains, absence of systemic TB signs, and lack of Mycobacterium on histology. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included... tuberculosis... Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli..."
3. Mucosal neuromas considered due to nodular tongue lesions; excluded by histology showing granulomatous inflammation rather than proliferative neural tissue. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included... mucosal neuromas... Histopathological examination... revealed... well‑formed epithelioid granulomas."
4. Sarcoidosis considered because of non‑caseating granulomas; excluded by endemic setting, positive rK‑39 serology, and eventual PCR confirmation of Leishmania. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included... sarcoidosis... Although rK‑39 serology was positive, its limited sensitivity in mucosal PKDL necessitated molecular confirmation."

case_prompt: A middle‑aged male farmer presented with a recurrent trophic ulcer over the forefoot that had persisted for four years. He had completed a course of multi‑drug therapy ten years earlier and had been free of active disease. Previous management at multiple centres—including walking cast, regular dressings, skin grafting, and fillet flaps from the great and second toes—had ultimately failed, and the ulcer recurred. On examination he had a large trophic ulcer involving the first, second, and third metatarsal‑head region. X‑ray demonstrated characteristic pencilling and tapering of the distal end of the metatarsal. Clinical assessment and handheld Doppler showed good flow in the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries. Sensation was reduced over the entire sole and foot. Debridement removed necrotic tissue and osteomyelitic bone. The resultant defect measured 7 cm × 6 cm, precluding use of a local flap. A 13‑cm‑long pedicle was required; therefore, a radial artery forearm flap from the right non‑dominant forearm was planned. The flap was raised under tourniquet control, with end‑to‑side anastomosis of the radial artery to the dorsalis pedis and end‑to‑end anastomosis of the cephalic vein to the venae comitantes; venous anastomosis was performed before the arterial anastomosis, and the donor site was split‑skin grafted.

case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old man from Sri Lanka presented with sudden onset breathlessness and right‑sided pleuritic chest pain. Five days earlier he had developed a painful swelling of his right leg while being treated in hospital for recurrent episodes of erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). He had a history of lepromatous leprosy diagnosed three years prior, treated with WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) for multibacillary leprosy, complicated by ENL and managed with oral prednisolone. Recurrent ENL persisted after completion of MDT, leading to a second course of MDT three months before admission. Three weeks before admission he started thalidomide 100 mg twice daily and prednisolone 15 mg daily for refractory ENL. He had no recent surgery, immobilization, malignancy, or family history of thrombosis.

On examination he was dyspneic at rest, without central cyanosis. He displayed leonine facies, generalized erythematous skin with multiple nodules, and his right leg was swollen with pitting ankle edema and normal arterial pulses. Neurologic exam revealed a glove‑and‑stocking peripheral sensory neuropathy. Abdominal exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed mild anemia, a normal white‑cell count and differential, and thrombocytopenia of 90 × 10³/µL that normalized after thalidomide withdrawal; liver and renal functions were normal. A computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) was ordered to evaluate his dyspnea.

2. Confirmed femoral deep vein thrombosis provides a thromboembolic source for emboli | "venous doppler ultrasound of the lower limb confirmed a deep vein thrombosis in the right femoral vein."

case_prompt:

case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old man with asthma, rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, and hypertension returned to the United States from a trip to Nigeria. One day after return he developed generalized weakness, intermittent fevers, nausea, vomiting, and mild abdominal pain. He denied use of herbal supplements.

He presented to the emergency department three days after symptom onset. He was hemodynamically stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed:
- Complete blood count, Plasmodium species antigen, Plasmodium falciparum antigen, and thick/thin blood smears: all negative.
- Respiratory infection PCR panel and hepatitis viral antigen/antibody panel: negative.
- AST 1,331 U/L (normal 10–50) and ALT 259 U/L (normal 5–50).
- Creatinine 2.57 mg/dL and BUN 29 mg/dL (normal BUN 8–23) indicating intrinsic AKI.
- Protein/creatinine ratio 74 mg/g (normal 0–30).

Abdominal ultrasound and CT showed no intra‑abdominal pathology. Chest X‑ray and abdominal CT revealed focal interstitial thickening and ground‑glass infiltrates in the left lower lung lobe, consistent with pneumonia.

The patient was admitted, started on atovaquone‑proguanil for possible malaria, and the following day received azithromycin and ceftriaxone for suspected pulmonary infection along with intravenous fluids for AKI. On hospital day 3 (two days after treatment initiation) his CK rose above 19,000 U/L, indicating rhabdomyolysis, and his liver enzymes worsened, prompting aggressive intravenous hydration.

Because of the worsening renal function and proteinuria, a percutaneous renal needle biopsy was performed. (Biopsy findings are reported in the article but are not included here.)

1. Malaria as the primary etiology – The patient had recent travel to a malaria‑endemic region, a prior diagnosis of malaria, incomplete antimalarial therapy, persistent fever, hepatic dysfunction, AKI, and rhabdomyolysis, all of which are recognized complications of severe malaria. | "Two days prior to leaving Nigeria, he noted the onset of intermittent fevers, was diagnosed with malarial infection, and was subsequently started on artemether‑lumefantrine… he discontinued his artemether‑lumefantrine course within the first two days of symptom onset."

Negative malaria diagnostics do not exclude infection – Initial rapid antigen tests and microscopy were negative, but the authors note that these results could reflect suppression of parasitemia after partial treatment. | "Complete blood counts, Plasmodium species antigen blood tests, Plasmodium falciparum antigen blood tests, light microscopy of thick and thin blood smears… were all unremarkable. These results indicated possible but unconfirmed suppression of malarial infection by the time of testing."
3. Pulmonary infection considered but not supported – Imaging showed infiltrates, yet respiratory PCR panel was negative and no focal infectious source was identified, making bacterial pneumonia less likely. | "Chest X‑ray revealed focal interstitial thickening and ground‑glass infiltrates… Respiratory infection PCR panel… were all unremarkable."
4. Viral hepatitis ruled out – Hepatitis viral antigen and antibody panels were negative despite marked transaminase elevation, arguing against viral hepatitis as the cause of liver injury. | "Hepatitis viral antigen and antibody panel were all unremarkable."

Drug‑induced toxicity considered – Azithromycin and ceftriaxone were started after admission, but the temporal sequence (CK elevation and AKI preceded antimicrobial therapy) makes drug toxicity unlikely. | "On the third day of the admission… he was found to have rhabdomyolysis… prompting aggressive hydration."

Rhabdomyolysis as a mechanism – Extremely high CK (>19,000 U/L) and subsequent renal biopsy showing myoglobin casts confirmed rhabdomyolysis, which can be precipitated by severe malaria. | "He was found to have rhabdomyolysis with creatine kinase (CK) level above 19,000 U/L… many tubular granular eosinophilic casts… which stained positively for myoglobin."
7. Acute kidney injury secondary to myoglobin casts – The biopsy demonstrated acute tubular injury with myoglobin casts, linking the AKI to rhabdomyolysis rather than primary glomerular disease. | "Evidence of acute tubular injury… there were many tubular granular eosinophilic casts… stained positively for myoglobin."

On exam she was mildly pallorous with mild epigastric tenderness; vital signs were stable and weight was 77 kg. A contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT scan performed three days after readmission demonstrated dilated bowel loops with mottled hypodensities in the caecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon, consistent with fecal impaction. case_prompt:
A 19‑year‑old male with no known comorbidities presented to an outside hospital with a two‑week history of high‑grade fever and a productive cough with scant expectoration. Chest radiograph demonstrated blunting of the right costophrenic angle consistent with a right‑sided pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant pleural fluid, and the patient was clinically diagnosed with pleural tuberculosis and started on four‑drug antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).  

During therapy the patient experienced significant drug‑related adverse effects requiring multiple regimen modifications. He subsequently developed a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure; brain MRI showed right frontal, temporal, parietal, cerebellar lesions, and phenytoin was initiated. Two months after starting therapy, repeat chest radiograph showed bilateral pleural effusions. A second thoracentesis again revealed an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant pleural fluid with a markedly elevated adenosine deaminase level (135.2 U/L). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for acid‑fast bacilli, and transbronchial lung biopsy showed ill‑defined epithelioid granulomas with inflammatory infiltrates.  

The patient was referred for persistent moderate‑to‑high‑grade fever, cough, worsening bilateral pleural effusions, and new epistaxis. Examination noted fever, tachycardia, cachexia, a florid petechial rash over the chest and abdomen, decreased bilateral chest expansion with reduced breath sounds, and hepatosplenomegaly. Contrast‑enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen demonstrated numerous miliary nodules throughout both lungs, bilateral pleural effusions, enlarged necrotic subcarinal and right hilar lymph nodes, multiple well‑defined hypodense lesions in the liver, spleen, and right kidney, and a large wedge‑shaped hypodense lesion in the posterior lower pole of the spleen.

During October 2012, a previously healthy 31‑year‑old Canadian man presented to a Toronto hospital after 3 days of fever and severe headache. He had returned 10 days earlier from a 10‑day work trip to South Sudan, where he did not use malaria chemoprophylaxis but slept under an insecticide‑treated net.  

Initial assessment showed a blood smear positive for *Plasmodium falciparum* with 22 % parasitemia (1,100,000 parasites/µL). Laboratory values were: bilirubin 88 µmol/L (ref 5‑17), AST 105 U/L (ref 10‑38), creatinine 130 µmol/L (ref 80‑115), hemoglobin 144 g/L (ref 140‑160), platelets 17 × 10⁹/L (ref 150‑450). He received one dose each of doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, and artemether/lumefantrine but vomited within an hour. He was transferred to a tertiary ICU for exchange transfusion and started on intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h) followed by a 3‑day oral atovaquone/proguanil course. Chest radiograph was normal, blood cultures were negative, and hemoglobin on admission was 125 g/L. Parasitemia became undetectable within 36 h, and he was discharged after 5 days.  

Four days after discharge, he returned with fever and “merlot‑colored” urine beginning 2 days after discharge. On re‑admission he was jaundiced. Labs showed bilirubin 89 µmol/L, LDH 1,976 U/L (ref 120‑240), hemoglobin 81 g/L, and marked hemoglobinuria; repeat thick and thin smears were negative for *Plasmodium*. Over the next days he required eight red‑cell transfusions to keep hemoglobin >75 g/L. Hemolysis persisted with a nadir hemoglobin of 68 g/L, LDH peak 3,429 U/L, and low haptoglobin (<0.12 g/L). Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase was normal. Hemolysis resolved spontaneously 10 days after onset. At 6‑week follow‑up he was asymptomatic with hemoglobin 135 g/L. Testing did not reveal red‑cell alloantibodies, and serology was positive for schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, and Q‑fever—considered past infections and not contributory.

2. G6PD deficiency evaluated and ruled out as “his glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase level was within reference range.”  
3. Ongoing malaria infection was excluded by negative blood smears: “multiple thick and thin blood smears were negative for *Plasmodium* spp.” and parasitemia had been undetectable within 36 h of the first admission.  
4. Prior parasitic/zoonotic infections (schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, Q‑fever) were deemed irrelevant: “Serologic tests showed that he was also positive for causative organisms… These diagnoses were consistent with past infections and were not considered to be contributory to the current severe hemolytic event.”  
5. Hemolysis due to other antimalarial agents (doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, artemether/lumefantrine) was deemed unlikely because “severe intravascular hemolysis has rarely been reported in relationship to these agents.”  
6. Drug‑induced immune hemolysis was considered but not substantiated: “We cannot exclude a potential role for drug‑induced immune hemolysis,” yet no alloantibodies or other immunologic markers were identified.

Left lower chest pain was continuous with radiation to the left shoulder. There was no associated cough, shortness of breath, altered bowel or bladder habits, jaundice, headache, vomiting, joint pain, or any skin nodules. case_prompt: A 48‑year‑old African man presented to Kinshasa University Hospital with persistent fever, dry cough, vomiting, myalgia, and generalized weakness since March 16, 2020. He self‑medicated with artemether‑lumefantrine for three days without improvement. On March 23, a blood smear showed *Plasmodium falciparum*; he received intravenous artesunate for five days plus cefixime. Two weeks after symptom onset, he developed anuria and presented to the emergency unit on April 2. Sixteen days earlier he had contact with a confirmed COVID‑19 case. Past medical history included type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension; baseline creatinine six months prior was 0.72 mg/dL with no proteinuria. On admission he was dyspneic (RR 23), BP 152/84 mmHg, SpO₂ 93%. Nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR. Laboratory studies revealed severe kidney dysfunction (urea 222 mg/dL, creatinine 15.9 mg/dL). Kidney ultrasound showed enlarged, echogenic kidneys with increased resistive index; no obstruction was seen. He was started on chloroquine, azithromycin, and vitamin C per national protocol. COVID‑19 PCR and malaria smear were negative on days 14 and 21. He required hemodialysis for anuric stage 3 AKI. After five dialysis sessions, diuresis increased to 4 L/day and creatinine fell to 2 mg/dL; the clinical diagnosis was acute tubular necrosis. On hospital day 27, after renal recovery, he developed full‑blown nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria (18 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dL), and dyslipidemia, while serum creatinine rose again to 13 mg/dL. No hypotensive episodes or nephrotoxic drugs were reported; renal‑vein thrombosis was excluded by ultrasound. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were negative. A percutaneous kidney biopsy on day 30 yielded three cores with 17 glomeruli. All but one glomerulus showed segmental or global collapse of the capillary tuft and enlargement of Bowman's space. Bowman’s space was lined by 1–3 layers of hypertrophic and hyperplastic epithelial cells, some with cytoplasmic vacuolization and occasional protein droplets. Early synechiae connecting glomeruli to Bowman's capsule were present. Tubular findings included severe injury with epithelial denudation, loss of brush border, cellular blebbing, mitoses, pronounced Ki‑67 positivity, microcystic dilatation, proteinaceous casts, and PAS‑positive resorption droplets. No tubulitis was seen. The interstitium exhibited mild edema, patchy moderate fibrosis, and a moderate to marked chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Arteries and arterioles were unremarkable.

1. Acute tubular necrosis was initially favored because of anuric AKI, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, and recovery after dialysis; the clinical diagnosis was stated as acute tubular necrosis. | "The clinical diagnosis was acute tubular necrosis."
2. Collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (collapsing glomerulopathy) was considered due to biopsy showing global/segmental glomerular collapse, hypertrophic epithelial cells, and proteinaceous casts. | "All but one displayed segmental or global collapse, implosion of the glomerular capillary tuft, and enlargement of Bowman space... Bowman space was occupied by hypertrophic and hyperplastic epithelial cells..."

4. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and CMV infections as causes of collapsing glomerulopathy were excluded by negative serologies. | "Serologic analyses for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were negative."
5. Drug‑induced or hypotension‑related renal injury was deemed unlikely because the patient had no episodes of hypotension and received no nephrotoxic drugs. | "There were no episodes of hypotension, and the patient received no nephrotoxic drugs."

There was no history of substance use, alcohol, smoking, or other comorbidities.

In an outside hospital, dengue NS1 antigen testing on day 3 of illness was positive, and the platelet count was 40 000/mm³. On arrival he was thin, pale, edematous, afebrile, mildly drowsy, and disoriented. Vital signs: HR 128 bpm (regular), BP 98/60 mm Hg, RR 30/min, SpO₂ 86 % on room air (improved to 92‑95 % with 4 L O₂). Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting pedal edema and multiple palpable, non‑tender purpuric macules (2‑8 mm) on both feet with fine scaling and post‑inflammatory hyperpigmentation. case_prompt:
A 2‑month‑old infant was admitted in May 2018 to the children’s emergency department with a one‑month history of distressing, nocturnal cough and a three‑week history of high‑grade intermittent fever partially relieved by paracetamol. She was born at 28 weeks gestation by emergency lower‑segment Caesarean section after ante‑partum haemorrhage, weighing 1.65 kg, and had been managed in a special‑care baby unit for prematurity, neonatal sepsis, and jaundice before discharge at 1.8 kg. On presentation she appeared acutely ill, febrile (38.6 °C), mildly pale, dyspnoeic and tachypnoeic (RR 66/min) with SpO₂ 80 % on room air, heart rate 186 bpm. Weight was 3.7 kg (3rd percentile); length 50 cm and head circumference 38 cm (both <3rd percentile). Examination revealed tender hepatomegaly (6 cm) and splenomegaly (6 cm). Laboratory studies showed PCV 21 %, random glucose 4.7 mmol/L, HIV screen negative, total WBC 12.6 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 65 %, lymphocytes 33 %), platelets 179 × 10⁹/L, malaria parasite test positive, Gene Xpert negative, Mantoux 0 mm. Chest X‑ray demonstrated hazy opacities in the right upper and middle lobes, left upper lobe opacities, and pneumatoceles. She received oxygen at 2 L/min and a transfusion of 60 mL settled cells (post‑transfusion PCV 25 %). Initial treatment included IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin; fever subsided and respiratory rate improved, and she was discharged after five days.

One week later she returned with worsening cough, fever, and respiratory distress. A provisional diagnosis of septicaemia with heart failure was made, with differential considerations of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and pulmonary tuberculosis. Empiric therapy was started with IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin, and oral azithromycin; furosemide and digoxin were added. On day 2, IV cloxacillin replaced gentamicin; on day 3 the child developed two generalized tonic‑clonic seizures lasting 1–2 min each, the second aborted with IV diazepam. Random glucose at the time was 2.9 mmol/L and SpO₂ fell to 67 %. Phenobarbitone and cautious IV fluids were commenced; supportive measures included repeat blood transfusion, nil per oral, oxygen, continued diuretics and digoxin. CSF analysis was not consistent with meningitis. Despite maximal therapy the infant remained in severe respiratory distress with intermittent hypothermia and died five days after readmission. Blood cultures were obtained on admission and on day 3 of the second stay (results were pending at the time of death).

Bacterial sepsis from common pathogens (e.g., Gram‑negative rods) presumed, leading to empiric ceftriaxone, gentamicin, cloxacillin, but the lack of clinical improvement suggested an atypical or resistant organism. | "Empirical antibiotic (IV Ceftriaxone, IV Gentamicin, Suspension Azithromax) therapy were commenced."
5. Meningitis considered after seizures; CSF was “not in keeping with meningitis,” reducing its likelihood. | "CSF analysis was not in keeping with meningitis."
6. HIV infection excluded by “HIV screening was negative,” removing opportunistic infections from differential. | "HIV screening was negative"
7. The eventual identification of *T. ptyseos* from blood cultures (reported after death) provided the definitive etiologic agent, explaining persistent sepsis despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Blood culture yielded T. ptyseos."

case_prompt:
A 12‑year‑old girl presented with a one‑month history of sudden‑onset, progressively worsening headache associated with multiple episodes of vomiting and intermittent fever. There was no rash, seizure, loss of consciousness, or known contact with tuberculosis patients. Past medical history was unremarkable.

On examination she appeared ill. Vital signs: HR 64/min, RR 30/min, Temp 37.1 °C, BP 90/60 mm Hg. Chest exam revealed bilateral vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. Cardiovascular exam noted a pansystolic murmur. Abdomen was soft with mild hepatomegaly (2 cm). Neurologic assessment: GCS 14/15, pupils reactive 4 mm, early papilledema on funduscopy, flaccid tone, 4/5 strength in all limbs, intact sensation, grade II reflexes, downgoing plantar responses, and positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Working diagnosis was meningitis.

Laboratory studies: Hb 13.2 g/dL, WBC 13 000/mm³ (neutrophils 85 %, lymphocytes 10 %), platelets 211 000/mm³, ESR 31 mm/hr. Renal panel showed BUN 30 mg/dL, creatinine 0.46 mg/dL. HIV, HBsAg, and HCV serologies were negative. Chest x‑ray demonstrated bilateral consolidation; abdominal ultrasound confirmed mild hepatomegaly. MRI brain showed leptomeningeal enhancement and mild thickening without basal exudates or hydrocephalus, suggestive of meningoencephalitis. Echocardiogram identified a perimembranous ventricular septal defect (12 mm) partially closed by the tricuspid valve with mild tricuspid regurgitation.

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 27 cm H₂O. CSF analysis – RBC 3 (0), WBC 204 (neutrophils 5 %, lymphocytes 95 %), glucose 46 mg/dL, protein 24 mg/dL, ADA 2.1 U/L. Gram stain, AFB stain, India‑ink preparation, and cultures were negative; cryptococcal antigen testing was unavailable. Blood and urine cultures were negative.

Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone 1.5 g IV q12h and vancomycin 100 mg IV q6h was started for 7 days. During this period she had a single seizure treated with antiepileptics and required supplemental oxygen. No clinical improvement occurred, and she was transferred to a second hospital.

On admission to the second facility she was semiconscious and admitted to the pediatric ICU. Additional investigations performed included leptospira IgM, brucella IgM, malaria antigen, and Mantoux tuberculin skin test, all of which were negative. Blood and urine cultures remained sterile, and sputum AFB smear and culture were negative. GeneXpert testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was not available.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis considered initially due to acute headache and fever but deemed unlikely because CSF showed a lymphocyte‑predominant pleocytosis, normal protein, low opening pressure, and all cultures were negative. | "CSF ... A 53‑year‑old morbidly obese female with hypertension presented to the emergency department with sudden loss of consciousness, left‑sided weakness, and altered sensorium for two days, accompanied by high‑grade fever and vomiting. Admission labs are summarized in Table 1 (not reproduced here). ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia; chest X‑ray was normal.  

After several ICU days she developed high‑grade fevers (core temperature 106‑107 °F), rhabdomyolysis (CK ≈ 10,000 IU/L), stage III acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy, and coagulopathy necessitating blood products. Cultures remained sterile, and drug‑induced hyperthermia was excluded. A repeat head CT showed no hematoma expansion. Workup for COVID‑19 was negative. Given a prior history of fever with chills and myalgia one week before admission, a tropical workup was ordered for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus.

case_prompt:
A 24‑year‑old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department after several weeks of progressive headache, gait imbalance, and horizontal diplopia. He denied foreign travel or unusual dietary exposures. He was born 5 weeks premature but otherwise had an uncomplicated neonatal course; there was no family history of neurologic or metabolic disease.

Neurologic examination revealed a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia and decreased sensation to light touch, pinprick, and temperature in the left arm. Neuro‑ophthalmologic assessment showed no retinal telangiectasias.

Non‑contrast head CT demonstrated dense calcifications in the left corona radiata and bilateral thalami, a 3.7 × 2.4 × 2.5 cm cyst within the pons compressing the fourth ventricle, and resultant ventriculomegaly. The cyst wall showed a 4‑mm mural enhancement on the right anterior aspect. Subsequent MRI confirmed these findings and additionally showed extensive periventricular and pericyst FLAIR hyperintensity.

Serologic testing for cysticercosis returned negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurocysticercosis considered because of a solitary cystic brainstem lesion with mural enhancement and surrounding edema, a pattern typical of viable cysticercal cysts; “Serologic study for cysticercosis was negative” indicates this diagnosis was specifically investigated. |
2. Neoplastic lesion (e.g., low‑grade glioma) entertained due to mass effect and enhancement, but excluded by pathology showing “no evidence of neoplastic processes.” |
3. Vascular malformation (angioma) considered given enhancement, yet ruled out because “No angiomatous rearrangement of microvasculature” was observed. |
4. Pilocytic astrocytoma or other glial tumor considered (often associated with Rosenthal fibers), but excluded as “No Rosenthal fibers were noted in the cyst wall.” |
5. Non‑parasitic cystic entities (e.g., epidermoid, arachnoid cyst) were less likely given the presence of mural enhancement and green cystic fluid described intraoperatively, features atypical for those lesions.

case_prompt: A 40‑year‑old man presented with a 4‑month history of progressive visual loss in the right eye, beginning with pain and culminating in complete blindness within 6 weeks. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasonography were unremarkable, and there was no significant lymphadenopathy. Infiltrations from lymphomatosis, gliomatosis, and other compressive optic neuropathies were deemed less likely, especially in view of the brain lesions. Because the optic nerve remained markedly enhancing, a decision was made to obtain tissue for definitive diagnosis, with options of optic nerve versus brain biopsy.

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 23‑year‑old man presented with fever, occasional headache and vomiting for 4 days, and one episode of generalized tonic‑clonic seizure 2 days prior to admission, followed by altered sensorium and left‑sided weakness. On arrival he was afebrile, not opening eyes to painful stimuli. Neurological examination showed Glasgow Coma Scale 7/15 (E1V2M4) with left hemiparesis, asymmetric non‑reactive pupils, restricted extra‑ocular movements, and blurred disc margins on fundus examination. Deep‑tendon reflexes were brisk; plantar response was extensor on the left and flexor on the right. Routine hematology and biochemistry were normal. Serologies for HIV, HBsAg, homocysteine, rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody were negative. Lumbar puncture was contraindicated. ECG demonstrated T‑wave depression in leads V1‑V4. Chest X‑ray showed inhomogeneous opacities in the left mid and lower zones with bilateral hilar prominence. 

Cranial CT revealed a hemorrhagic lesion in the right thalamus and right medial temporal lobe with multiple cerebral and cerebellar ring‑enhancing lesions. MRI brain demonstrated heterogeneous mixed‑signal intensity changes in the right thalamus, caudate and medial temporal region consistent with hemorrhagic infarct and extensive perilesional edema extending into the internal and external capsules and corona radiata. Lesions bloomed on flash 2D sequences, indicating paramagnetic substances from evolving hemorrhage. Iso‑ to hyper‑intense T1 and predominantly hypo‑intense T2 lesions in the right cerebral peduncle suggested tuberculoma. Diffusion‑weighted imaging showed hyper‑intensity (facilitated diffusion) in the right thalamus, medial temporal region and midbrain, and hypo‑intensity (restricted diffusion) in the pons. Hemorrhage extended into the lateral ventricles of both occipital horns. The third and lateral ventricles were dilated with minimal periventricular hyper‑intensity, indicating uncompensated hydrocephalus. Multiple rounded lesions iso‑intense on T1 and hypo‑intense on T2 were noted in the left pons, bilateral parasagittal basifrontal zones and left posterior‑medial parietal lobe, suggestive of tuberculous granulomas. FLAIR imaging showed diffuse sulcal hyper‑intensity consistent with meningitis. MR venogram demonstrated non‑visualization of the bilateral internal cerebral veins, vein of Rosenthal, vein of Galen, proximal straight sinus and left transverse sinus.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculoma (tuberculosis) considered because imaging showed ring‑enhancing lesions with T1 iso‑/hyper‑intensity and T2 hypointensity, “suggestive of tuberculoma,” and later acid‑fast organisms were identified. | "Smear from the basal exudates of the brain revealed acid fast organisms by Ziehl‑Neelsen stain."
2. Cerebral toxoplasmosis was a differential given the multiple ring‑enhancing lesions, but was excluded by negative serology and lack of Toxoplasma organisms. | "Possibility of cerebral toxoplasmosis was also considered in view of multiple ring enhancing lesions." … "Serum and CSF samples collected at autopsy were negative for IgG/IgM antibody to ... Toxoplasma gondii."
3. Neurocysticercosis was considered as a possible cause of ring‑enhancing lesions, but serology was negative and histology showed caseating granulomas rather than cysticerci. | "Serum and CSF samples collected at autopsy were negative for ... Cysticercosis."
4. Vascular causes (arterial ischemia, hemorrhagic infarct) were entertained due to diffusion and hemorrhage patterns, yet the distribution corresponded to venous drainage territories and venous thrombosis was demonstrated on MR venogram, supporting a venous etiology secondary to tuberculous phlebitis. | "MR venogram revealed non‑visualization of the bilateral internal cerebral veins, vein of Rosenthal, vein of Galen and proximal segment of straight sinus and left transverse sinus."
5. Pulmonary infection was suggested by chest X‑ray opacities and hilar prominence, aligning with the systemic tuberculosis diagnosis. | "Chest X‑ray revealed inhomogeneous opacities in the left mid and lower zones with bilateral hilar prominence."

case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old agricultural laborer was admitted to the neurology service with a 1‑year history of three generalized tonic‑clonic seizures, irritability, bursts of anger, abusive behavior, and inability to recognize close relatives, together with a 7‑day history of fever and headache. Three days after fever onset he developed altered sensorium and urinary incontinence, and on the day of admission he noted new right‑sided weakness.

On examination the patient was febrile; vital signs otherwise were normal. Neurological assessment showed a Glasgow Coma Scale of 6/15 (E1V2M3), right hemiparesis, lack of eye opening to deep painful stimuli, restricted extra‑ocular movements with papilledema, non‑reactive, dilated pupils, brisk deep tendon reflexes, an extensor plantar response on the right and flexor on the left.

Laboratory studies revealed a total leukocyte count of 15,200 cells/µL and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated; HIV and hepatitis B tests were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 170 cells/mm³ (80 % polymorphonuclear), protein 117 mg/dL, and glucose 11 mg/dL. 

Cranial computed tomography demonstrated multiple disc‑enhancing lesions in both grey and white matter and the brain stem, accompanied by edema and hydrocephalus. Magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple subcortical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal white matter, as well as in the pons and midbrain. A few well‑defined T2‑hypointense lesions suggestive of small tuberculomas were noted in the bilateral frontal subcortical regions. Additional findings included heterogeneous signal in the left thalamus and caudate nucleus, lesions that bleeded on gradient imaging, mixed diffusion patterns, and thrombosed cortical veins appearing as hypointense curvilinear structures on FLAIR.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) – supported by imaging features consistent with tuberculomas and later confirmed by microbiologic evidence. | "A few well defined T2 hypointense lesions suggestive of small tuberculomas were also noted" and "Smear from the basal exudate revealed numerous acid fast organisms on Zeihl‑Neelson stain."
2. Cerebral toxoplasmosis – considered because ring‑enhancing lesions can be seen in toxoplasmosis, especially in endemic regions. | "Possibility of cerebral toxoplasmosis and cysticercosis were also considered in view of ring enhancing lesions and the endemicity."
3. Neurocysticercosis – considered for the same radiologic reason of ring‑enhancing lesions. | "Possibility of cerebral toxoplasmosis and cysticercosis were also considered in view of ring enhancing lesions and the endemicity."
4. Exclusion of toxoplasmosis and cysticercosis – serologic testing was negative for both pathogens, decreasing their likelihood. | "Post mortem serum and CSF were positive for mycobacterial antibody and IgG and IgM type mycobacterial immune complex and negative for cysticercosis and toxoplasmosis."
5. Exclusion of other bacterial meningitis – CSF showed a predominance of polymorphonuclear cells with low glucose, but lack of Gram‑stain organisms and presence of acid‑fast bacilli favored mycobacterial infection over typical pyogenic bacteria. | (Implicit in CSF description and later acid‑fast findings.)
